subject: Cooking
title: The Food Truck Revolution
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Food Truck Revolution.

hook.text: In 2008, a Korean-Mexican taco truck in LA tweeted its location. Lines stretched around blocks. A revolution began.

buildup.text: Roy Choi's Kogi BBQ truck used Twitter to announce locations — merging street food with social media.

discovery.text: Food trucks exploded globally — chefs who couldn't afford restaurants launched mobile kitchens instead.

twist.text: Some food truck chefs later opened brick-and-mortar restaurants — the truck was the audition, not the career.

climax.text: The US food truck industry alone is now worth $1.4 billion — with 35,000 trucks nationwide.

punchline.text: A tweet about tacos launched a $1.4 billion industry.

quiz.question: What innovation did Kogi BBQ introduce to street food?
options: Using social media to announce truck locations

details.summary: The food truck revolution transformed urban dining by bringing chef-driven cuisine to streets, office parks, and festivals. Cities rewrote zoning laws to accommodate trucks. Food truck parks emerged as permanent installations.
details.whyItMatters: Food trucks disrupted the traditional restaurant model by proving that quality food, creative menus, and direct customer relationships can work outside conventional brick-and-mortar spaces.
takeaways: Cities rewrote zoning laws to accommodate the food truck boom
Food truck parks became permanent dining destinations
Lower risk enabled more diverse and experimental cuisine

faq.question: Why do some cities resist food trucks?
faq.answer: Restaurant owners lobby against trucks that park nearby and compete without paying rent. Health departments worry about inspection challenges. Neighbors complain about traffic and litter. Many cities created designated zones and strict permit systems as compromise solutions.

faq.question: Can food trucks become full restaurants?
faq.answer: Many successful trucks graduate to brick-and-mortar locations once they build a loyal following. The truck serves as low-risk market testing. If a concept works from a truck, it likely works with a lease. Some operators keep both to serve different markets simultaneously.
